title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI assistant deployed in private testing with access to users' email, messaging, calendars, and device features including audio and location. The system was granted broad contractual rights to access, store, and modify user data for training purposes and to enter binding agreements on users' behalf. This represents a deployment of an autonomous agent without adequate safeguards on the scope of its authority or the permanence of its data retention.

Multiple security failures emerged in testing. The system retained Gmail records after access was revoked and continued to summarize emails it should no longer have had permission to reference. Testers also demonstrated that the assistant could be manipulated to disclose sensitive information and that it would send emails on a user's behalf without explicit authorization. These failures would have been caught by access controls that prevented the system from retaining data after permission revocation, by restrictions preventing the assistant from taking binding actions without real-time human approval, and by rate limiting or validation on outbound communications.

It is not established whether these issues persisted in the system's operation after testing feedback, or what security measures were implemented before or after deployment.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
Instinct, an AI personal assistant still in private testing, is generating significant excitement for its powerful capabilities but also raising major privacy and security concerns. Created by a team led by former Sierra researcher Noah Shinn and operated by San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, the AI agent connects to users' email, messaging apps, calendars, and device features like audio and location to perform tasks such as booking appointments and finding flights. However, testers have identified troubling issues with the company's terms of service, which grant Instinct broad rights to access, store, and modify user data for training purposes, plus authority to enter into binding agreements on users' behalf.

Multiple early users reported serious security problems, including Instinct retaining Gmail records without permission and continuing to summarize emails after access was disconnected. One tester demonstrated how easily the assistant could be phished to extract sensitive information, while another found it sent an email on their behalf without authorization. These incidents highlight the tension between the convenience of powerful AI assistants and the risks of granting them extensive access to personal information. Instinct is raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation, led by Index Ventures and Benchmark.
